title: VIII. Delirium
paragraphs: What followed was almost an orgy, a feast to which everyone was welcome. Grushenka was the first to call for wine.
“I want to drink. I want to be completely drunk, the way we were before. Do you remember, Mitya, do you remember how we made friends here last time!”
Mitya himself was almost delirious, feeling that his happiness was at hand. But Grushenka kept sending him away from her.

“Go and enjoy yourself. Tell them to dance, to have a good time, ‘let the stove and cottage dance,' the way we had it last time,” she kept exclaiming. She was tremendously excited. And Mitya hurried to obey her. The chorus was in the next room. The room where they had been sitting until that moment was too small and was divided in two by cotton curtains, behind which stood a huge bed with a puffy feather mattress and a pyramid of cotton pillows. There were beds in each of the four rooms reserved for visitors. Grushenka settled herself right by the door. Mitya placed an easy chair for her. She had sat in the same spot to watch the dancing and singing “the time before,” when they had made merry there. All the girls who came had been there then; the Jewish band with fiddles and zithers had come too, and at last the long-expected cart had arrived with the wines and provisions.

Mitya bustled about. All sorts of people began coming into the room to watch—peasants and their wives, who had been roused from sleep and drawn by the hope of another marvelous entertainment like the one they had enjoyed a month earlier. Mitya remembered their faces, greeting and embracing everyone he knew. He uncorked bottles and poured out wine for everyone who stepped forward. Only the girls were really eager for the champagne. The men preferred rum, brandy, and, above all, hot punch. Mitya had chocolate made for all the girls and ordered that three samovars be kept boiling all night so that anyone could help themselves to tea and punch.

An absurd, chaotic confusion followed, but Mitya was in his natural element, and the sillier it became, the higher his spirits rose. If the peasants had asked him for money at that moment, he would have pulled out his notes and given them away right and left. That was probably why the landlord, Trifon Borissovitch, kept hovering near Mitya to protect him. He seemed to have given up all idea of going to bed that night, though he drank little—only one glass of punch—and kept a sharp eye on Mitya's interests in his own way. He stepped in just in time, civilly and obsequiously persuading Mitya not to give away “cigars and Rhine wine,” and above all money, to the peasants as he had done before. He was also very indignant about the peasant girls drinking liqueur and eating sweets.
“They're a lousy lot, Dmitri Fyodorovitch,” he said. “I'd give every one of them a kick, and they'd take it as an honor—that's all they're worth!”

Mitya remembered Andrey again and ordered punch to be sent out to him. “I was rude to him just now,” he repeated, his voice sinking, softened. Kalganov didn't want to drink, and at first didn't care for the girls' singing; but after he'd had a couple of glasses of champagne, he became extraordinarily lively, strolling around the room, laughing, praising the music and the songs, admiring everyone and everything. Maximov, blissfully drunk, never left his side. Grushenka, too, was starting to get drunk. Pointing to Kalganov, she said to Mitya:
“What a dear, charming boy he is!”

And Mitya, delighted, ran to kiss Kalganov and Maximov. Oh, his hopes were immense! She had said nothing yet, and seemed, in fact, to be deliberately holding back. But she looked at him from time to time with caressing, passionate eyes. At last she suddenly gripped his hand and pulled him vigorously toward her. She was sitting just then in the low chair by the door.
“How was it you came in just now, hm? Did you walk in? I was frightened. So you meant to give me up to him, did you? Did you really mean it?”
“I didn't want to spoil your happiness!” Mitya faltered blissfully. But she didn't need his answer.
“Well, go and enjoy yourself—” she sent him away once more. “Don't cry, I'll call you back again.”

He would run off, and she listened to the singing and watched the dancing, though her eyes followed him wherever he went. But in another quarter of an hour she would call him back again, and again he would come running.
“Come, sit beside me, tell me, how did you hear about me, and that I was coming here yesterday? Who did you first hear it from?”
And Mitya began telling her all about it, disconnectedly, incoherently, feverishly. He spoke strangely, often frowning and breaking off abruptly.
“What are you frowning at?” she asked.
“Nothing. I left a man ill back there. I'd give ten years of my life for him to recover—just to know he was all right!”

“Well, never mind him if he's ill. So you meant to shoot yourself tomorrow! What a silly boy! What for? I like reckless fellows like you,” she lisped, her tongue a little thick. “So you'd go to any lengths for me, would you? Did you really mean to shoot yourself tomorrow, you stupid? No, wait a little. Tomorrow I may have something to say to you. I won't say it today, but tomorrow. You'd like it to be today? No, I don't want to today. Come, go along now, go and amuse yourself.”
Once, though, she called him back with a puzzled, uneasy look.

“Why are you sad? I see you're sad. Yes, I see it,” she added, looking intently into his eyes. “Even though you keep kissing the peasants and shouting, I see something. No, be merry. I'm merry; you be merry too. I love somebody here. Guess who it is. Ah, look, my boy has fallen asleep, poor dear, he's drunk.”

She meant Kalganov. He was, in fact, drunk and had dropped asleep for a moment sitting on the sofa. But he wasn't just drowsy from drink; he had suddenly felt dejected, or, as he put it, “bored.” He was intensely depressed by the girls' songs, which, as the drinking went on, gradually grew coarser and more reckless. The dances were just as bad. Two girls dressed up as bears, and a lively girl called Stepanida, with a stick in her hand, played the part of keeper and began to “show them off.”
“Look alive, Marya, or you'll get the stick!”
The bears finally rolled on the ground in the most unseemly fashion, amid roars of laughter from the tightly packed crowd of men and women.
“Well, let them! Let them!” said Grushenka sententiously, with an ecstatic expression. “When they do get a day to enjoy themselves, why shouldn't folks be happy?”
Kalganov looked as though he had been splattered with dirt.
“It's swinish, all this peasant foolery,” he murmured, moving away. “It's the sort of thing they play when it's light all night in summer.”
He particularly disliked one “new” song set to a jaunty dance tune. It described a gentleman coming to try his luck with the girls, to see whether they would love him:
The master came to try the girls: Would they love him, would they not?
But the girls couldn't love the master:
He would beat me cruelly And such love won't do for me.
Then a gypsy comes along, and he too tries:
The gypsy came to try the girls: Would they love him, would they not?
But they couldn't love the gypsy either:
He would be a thief, I fear, And would cause me many a tear.
And many more men come to try their luck, among them a soldier:
The soldier came to try the girls: Would they love him, would they not?
But the soldier is rejected with contempt, in two indecent lines sung with absolute frankness and producing a furore in the audience. The song ends with a merchant:
The merchant came to try the girls: Would they love him, would they not?
And it turns out that he wins their love because:
The merchant will make gold for me And his queen I'll gladly be.
Kalganov was genuinely indignant.

“That's just a song from yesterday,” he said out loud. “Who writes such things for them? They might just as well have had a railwayman or a Jew come to try his luck with the girls—they'd have carried the day.”

And, almost as though it were a personal affront, he declared on the spot that he was bored, sat down on the sofa, and immediately fell asleep. His pretty little face looked rather pale as it fell back against the sofa cushion.
“Look how pretty he is,” said Grushenka, taking Mitya over to him. “I was combing his hair just now; his hair's like flax, and so thick—”
And, bending over him tenderly, she kissed his forehead. Kalganov instantly opened his eyes, looked at her, stood up, and with the most anxious air asked where Maximov was.
“So that's who you want.” Grushenka laughed. “Stay with me a minute. Mitya, go and find his Maximov.”

Maximov, it turned out, couldn't tear himself away from the girls, only running off now and then to pour himself a glass of liqueur. He had drunk two cups of chocolate. His face was red, his nose was crimson, his eyes were moist and mawkishly sweet. He ran up and announced that he was going to dance the “sabotière.”
“They taught me all those well-bred, aristocratic dances when I was little—”
“Go on, go with him, Mitya, and I'll watch from here how he dances,” said Grushenka.

“No, no, I'm coming to watch too,” exclaimed Kalganov, brushing aside in the most naïve way Grushenka's offer to sit with him. They all went to watch. Maximov danced his dance. But it roused no great admiration in anyone except Mitya. It consisted of nothing but skipping and hopping, kicking up his feet, and at every skip Maximov slapped the upturned sole of his foot. Kalganov didn't like it at all, but Mitya kissed the dancer.
“Thanks. Are you tired, perhaps? What are you looking for here? Would you like some sweets? A cigar, maybe?”
“A cigarette.”
“Don't you want a drink?”
“I'll just have a liqueur. Do you have any chocolates?”
“Yes, there's a heap of them on the table over there. Choose one, my dear soul!”
“I like one with vanilla—for old people. Heh heh!”
“No, brother, we don't have any of that special kind.”
“Listen,” the old man bent down to whisper in Mitya's ear, “that girl over there, little Marya, heh heh! How would it be if you helped me make friends with her?”
“So that's what you're after! No, brother, that won't do!”
“I'd do no harm to anyone,” Maximov muttered disconsolately.
“Oh, all right, all right. They only come here to dance and sing, you know, brother. But damn it all, wait a bit! Eat and drink and be merry in the meantime. Do you want money?”
“Later on, perhaps,” Maximov smiled.
“All right, all right—”

Mitya's head was burning. He stepped out onto the wooden balcony that ran all around the inside of the building, overlooking the courtyard. The fresh air revived him. He stood alone in a dark corner and suddenly clutched his head in both hands. His scattered thoughts came together; his sensations fused into a whole and threw a sudden light into his mind. A fearful and terrible light! “If I'm going to shoot myself, why not now?” passed through his mind. “Why not go for the pistols, bring them here, and here, in this dark, dirty corner, put an end to it?” For almost a minute he stood undecided. A few hours earlier, when he had been racing here, he was pursued by disgrace, by the theft he had committed, and that blood, that blood! And yet it had been easier for him then. Then everything was over: he had lost her, given her up. She was gone, for him—oh, then his death sentence had been easier; at least it had seemed necessary, inevitable, for what did he have to stay on earth for?

But now? Was it the same as then? Now one phantom, one terror at least was finished: that first, rightful lover, that fateful figure had vanished without a trace. The terrible phantom had turned into something so small, so comic; it had been carried into the bedroom and locked in. It would never return. She was ashamed, and from her eyes he could see now whom she loved. Now he had everything to make life happy—but he couldn't go on living, he couldn't; oh, damnation! “O God! Restore to life the man I knocked down at the fence! Let this fearful cup pass from me! Lord, You have worked miracles for sinners like me! But what, what if the old man's alive? Oh, then I would wipe away the shame of the other disgrace. I'd restore the stolen money. I'd give it back; I'd get it somehow. No trace of that shame will remain, except in my heart forever! But no, no; oh, impossible, cowardly dreams! Oh, damnation!”

Yet there was a ray of light and hope in his darkness. He jumped up and ran back to the room—to her, to her, his queen forever! Wasn't one moment of her love worth all the rest of life, even in the agonies of disgrace? This wild question clutched at his heart. “To her, to her alone, to see her, to hear her, to think of nothing, to forget everything, if only for that night, for an hour, for a moment!” Just as he turned from the balcony into the passage, he ran into the landlord, Trifon Borissovitch. He thought he looked gloomy and worried, and fancied he had come looking for him.
“What is it, Trifon Borissovitch? Are you looking for me?”
“No, sir.” The landlord seemed disconcerted. “Why should I be looking for you? Where have you been?”
“Why do you look so glum? You're not angry, are you? Wait a bit, you'll be in bed soon. What's the time?”
“It'll be three o'clock. Past three, it must be.”
“We'll stop soon. We'll stop.”
“Don't mention it; it's nothing. Keep it up as long as you like—”

“What's the matter with him?” Mitya wondered for a moment, and he ran back to the room where the girls were dancing. But she wasn't there. She wasn't in the blue room either; there was no one but Kalganov, asleep on the sofa. Mitya peeked behind the curtain—she was there. She was sitting in the corner, on a trunk. Bent forward, with her head and arms on the bed next to it, she was crying bitterly, doing her utmost to stifle her sobs so she wouldn't be heard. Seeing Mitya, she beckoned to him, and when he hurried over she grasped his hand tightly.

“Mitya, Mitya, I loved him, you know. How I loved him these five years, all that time! Did I love him, or just my own anger? No, him, him! It's a lie that it was my anger I loved and not him. Mitya, I was only seventeen then; he was so kind to me, so merry; he used to sing to me. Or so it seemed to a silly girl like me. And now, O Lord, it's not the same man. Even his face isn't the same; he's different altogether. I wouldn't have recognized him. I drove here with Timofey, and the whole way I was thinking how I'd meet him, what I'd say to him, how we'd look at one another. My soul was faint, and all at once it was as though he'd emptied a pail of dirty water over me. He talked to me like a schoolmaster, all so grave and learned; he met me so solemnly I was struck dumb. I couldn't get a word in. At first I thought he was ashamed to talk in front of his great big Pole. I sat staring at him, wondering why I couldn't say a word to him now. It must have been his wife that ruined him; you know he threw me over to get married. She must have changed him like that. Mitya, how shameful it is! Oh, Mitya, I'm ashamed, I'm ashamed for my whole life. Curse it, curse it, curse those five years!”
And again she burst into tears, but clung tight to Mitya's hand and wouldn't let it go.

“Mitya, darling, stay, don't go away. I want to tell you one thing,” she whispered, and suddenly raised her face to him. “Listen, tell me who it is I love? I love one man here. Who is that man? That's what you have to tell me.”
A smile lit up her face that was swollen from weeping, and her eyes shone in the half darkness.

“A falcon flew in, and my heart sank. ‘Fool! that's the man you love!' That was what my heart whispered to me at once. You came in, and everything grew bright. What's he afraid of? I wondered. For you were frightened; you couldn't speak. It's not them he's afraid of—could you be frightened of anyone? It's me he's afraid of, I thought, only me. So Fenya told you, you little fool, how I called out to Alyosha from the window that I'd loved Mityenka for one hour, and was now going to love—another. Mitya, Mitya, how could I be such a fool as to think I could love anyone after you? Do you forgive me, Mitya? Do you forgive me or not? Do you love me? Do you love me?” She jumped up and held him with both hands on his shoulders. Mitya, dumb with rapture, gazed into her eyes, at her face, at her smile, and suddenly clasped her tightly in his arms and kissed her passionately.

“You will forgive me for having tormented you? It was out of spite that I tormented you all. It was out of spite I drove the old man out of his mind. Do you remember how you drank at my house one day and broke the wineglass? I remembered that, and I broke a glass today and drank ‘to my vile heart.' Mitya, my falcon, why don't you kiss me? He kissed me once, and now he draws back and looks and listens. Why listen to me? Kiss me, kiss me hard, that's right. If you love, well then, love! I'll be your slave now, your slave for the rest of my life. It's sweet to be a slave. Kiss me! Beat me, mistreat me, do whatever you want with me. And I deserve to suffer. Stop, wait, afterwards, I don't want that—” she suddenly pushed him away. “Go along, Mitya, I'll come and have some wine, I want to be drunk, I'm going to get drunk and dance; I must, I must!” She tore herself away from him and disappeared behind the curtain. Mitya followed like a drunken man.

“Yes, come what may—whatever happens now, I'd give the whole world for one minute,” he thought. Grushenka did, in fact, toss back a whole glass of champagne in one gulp, and she became very tipsy at once. She sat down in the same chair as before, with a blissful smile on her face. Her cheeks were glowing, her lips were burning, her flashing eyes were moist; there was a passionate appeal in her gaze. Even Kalganov felt a stir in his heart and went over to her.

“Did you feel how I kissed you just now while you were asleep?” she said thickly. “I'm drunk now, that's what it is. And aren't you drunk? And why isn't Mitya drinking? Why don't you drink, Mitya? I'm drunk, and you don't drink—”
“I am drunk! I'm drunk as it is—drunk on you—and now I'll be drunk on wine too.”

He drank off another glass, and—he thought it strange himself—that glass made him completely drunk. He was suddenly drunk, even though up until that moment he had been quite sober; he remembered that. From that moment everything whirled around him, as though he were delirious. He walked, laughed, talked to everybody, without knowing what he was doing. Only one persistent, burning sensation made itself felt continually, “like a red-hot coal in his heart,” he said afterwards. He went over to her, sat beside her, gazed at her, listened to her. She became very talkative, kept calling everyone over, and beckoned to different girls out of the chorus. When a girl came up, she either kissed her or made the sign of the cross over her. In another minute she might start crying. She was greatly amused by the “little old man,” as she called Maximov. He ran up every minute to kiss her hands, “each little finger,” and finally he danced another dance to an old song, which he sang himself. He danced with special vigor to the refrain:

The little pig says—umph! umph! umph! The little calf says—moo, moo, moo, The little duck says—quack, quack, quack, The little goose says—ga, ga, ga. The hen goes strutting through the porch; Troo-roo-roo-roo-roo, she'll say, Troo-roo-roo-roo-roo, she'll say!

“Give him something, Mitya,” said Grushenka. “Give him a present, he's poor, you know. Ah, the poor, the insulted! Do you know, Mitya, I'm going into a nunnery. No, I really will one day. Alyosha said something to me today that I'll remember all my life. Yes. But today, let's dance. Tomorrow to the nunnery, but today we'll dance. I want to play today, good people, and what of it? God will forgive us. If I were God, I'd forgive everyone: ‘My dear sinners, from this day forth I forgive you.' I'm going to beg forgiveness: ‘Forgive me, good people, a silly wench.' I'm a beast, that's what I am. But I want to pray. I gave a little onion. Wicked as I've been, I want to pray. Mitya, let them dance, don't stop them. Everyone in the world is good. Everyone—even the worst of them. The world's a nice place. Though we're bad, the world's all right. We're good and bad, good and bad. Come, tell me, I've something to ask you: come here everyone, and I'll ask: Why am I so good? You know I'm good. I'm very good. Come, why am I so good?”

So Grushenka rambled on, getting more and more drunk. At last she announced that she was going to dance too. She got up from her chair, staggering. “Mitya, don't give me any more wine—if I ask, don't give me any. Wine doesn't bring peace. Everything's spinning, the stove, everything. I want to dance. Let everyone see how I dance—let them see how beautifully I dance—”

She really meant it. She pulled a white cambric handkerchief out of her pocket and took it by one corner in her right hand, to wave it in the dance. Mitya ran back and forth, the girls were quiet and got ready to break into a dancing song at the first signal. Maximov, hearing that Grushenka wanted to dance, squealed with delight and ran skipping about in front of her, humming:
With legs so slim and sides so trim And its little tail curled tight.
But Grushenka waved her handkerchief at him and drove him away.
“Shh! Mitya, why don't they come? Let everyone come—to watch. Call them in, too, the ones that were locked in. Why did you lock them in? Tell them I'm going to dance. Let them watch too—”
Mitya walked with a drunken swagger to the locked door and began knocking at the Poles with his fist.
“Hey, you Podvysotskys! Come on, she's going to dance. She's calling you.”
“_Lajdak!_” one of the Poles shouted back.
“You're a _lajdak_ yourself! You're a little scoundrel, that's what you are.”
“Stop making fun of Poland,” said Kalganov sententiously. He was drunk too.
“Be quiet, boy! Just because I call him a scoundrel doesn't mean I called all of Poland so. One _lajdak_ doesn't make a Poland. Be quiet, my pretty boy, eat a sweet.”

“Ach, what fellows! As though they weren't men. Why won't they make friends?” said Grushenka, and she stepped forward to dance. The chorus broke into “Ah, my porch, my new porch!” Grushenka flung back her head, half opened her lips, smiled, waved her handkerchief, and suddenly, with a violent lurch, stood still in the middle of the room, looking bewildered.
“I'm weak—” she said in an exhausted voice. “Forgive me. I'm weak, I can't. I'm sorry.”
She bowed to the chorus, then began bowing in every direction.
“I'm sorry. Forgive me—”
“The lady's been drinking. The pretty lady has been drinking,” voices were saying.
“The lady's drunk too much,” Maximov explained to the girls, giggling.
“Mitya, lead me away—take me,” said Grushenka helplessly. Mitya pounced on her, snatched her up in his arms, and carried his precious burden through the curtains.

“Well, now I'll go,” thought Kalganov, and walking out of the blue room, he closed the two halves of the door behind him. But the orgy in the larger room went on and grew louder and louder. Mitya laid Grushenka on the bed and kissed her on the lips.

“Don't touch me—” she faltered, in a pleading voice. “Don't touch me, until I'm yours. I've told you I'm yours, but don't touch me—spare me. With them here, with them so close, you mustn't. He's here. It's nasty here—”
“I'll obey you! I won't think of it—I worship you!” muttered Mitya. “Yes, it's nasty here, it's abominable.”
And still holding her in his arms, he sank to his knees by the bedside.

“I know, though you're a brute, you're generous,” Grushenka said with difficulty. “It must be honorable—it shall be honorable for the future—and let us be honest, let us be good, not brutes, but good. Take me away, take me far away, do you hear? I don't want it to be here, but far, far away—”
“Oh, yes, yes, it must be!” said Mitya, pressing her in his arms. “I'll take you and we'll fly away. Oh, I'd give my whole life for just one year of knowing about that blood!”
“What blood?” Grushenka asked, bewildered.
“Nothing,” muttered Mitya through his teeth. “Grusha, you wanted to be honest, but I'm a thief. I stole money from Katya. Disgrace, disgrace!”

“From Katya, from that young lady? No, you didn't steal it. Give it back to her, take it from me. Why make a fuss? Everything of mine is yours now. What does money matter? We'll waste it anyway. People like us are bound to waste money. But we'd better go and work the land. I want to dig the earth with my own hands. We have to work, do you hear? Alyosha said so. I won't be your mistress, I'll be faithful to you, I'll be your slave, I'll work for you. We'll go to the young lady and bow down before her together, so that she may forgive us, and then we'll go away. And if she won't forgive us, we'll go anyway. Take her her money, and love me. Don't love her. Don't love her any more. If you love her, I'll strangle her. I'll put out both her eyes with a needle—”
“I love you. I love only you. I'll love you in Siberia—”

“Why Siberia? Never mind, Siberia, if you like. I don't care—we'll work. There's snow in Siberia. I love driving through the snow—and we must have bells. Do you hear, there's a bell ringing? Where is that bell ringing? There are people coming. Now it's stopped.”

She closed her eyes, exhausted, and suddenly fell asleep for an instant. There had definitely been the sound of a bell in the distance, but the ringing had ceased. Mitya let his head sink onto her breast. He didn't notice that the bell had stopped, nor did he notice that the songs had ceased and that instead of singing and drunken clamor there was absolute stillness in the house. Grushenka opened her eyes.

“What's the matter? Was I asleep? Yes—a bell—I was asleep and dreamed I was driving through the snow with bells, and I dozed off. I was with someone I loved, with you. And far, far away. I was holding you and kissing you, nestling close. I was cold, and the snow glistened. You know how the snow glistens at night when the moon shines. It was as if I wasn't on earth. I woke up, and my dear one is close to me. How sweet that is!”

“Close to you,” murmured Mitya, kissing her dress, her bosom, her hands. And suddenly he had a strange sensation: it seemed to him that she was looking straight ahead, not at him, not into his face, but over his head, with an intent, almost uncanny fixity. An expression of wonder, almost of alarm, came suddenly into her face.
“Mitya, who is that looking at us?” she whispered.
Mitya turned and saw that someone had indeed parted the curtains and seemed to be watching them. And not just one person, it seemed.
He jumped up and walked quickly over to the intruder.
“Here, come over to us, come here,” said a voice, speaking not loudly, but firmly and with authority.

Mitya passed to the other side of the curtain and stood stock still. The room was filled with people, but not the ones who had been there before. An instantaneous shiver ran down his back, and he shuddered. He recognized everyone in an instant. That tall, stout old man in the overcoat and forage-cap with a cockade—was the police captain, Mihail Makarovitch. And that “consumptive-looking” trim dandy, “who always has such polished boots”—that was the deputy prosecutor. “He has a chronometer worth four hundred roubles; he showed it to me.” And that small young man in spectacles—Mitya forgot his surname, though he knew him, had seen him: he was the “investigating lawyer,” from the “school of jurisprudence,” who had only recently come to town. And this man—the inspector of police, Mavriky Mavrikyevitch, a man he knew well. And those fellows with the brass plates on—why are they here? And those other two—peasants. And there at the door stood Kalganov with Trifon Borissovitch.
“Gentlemen! What is this for, gentlemen?” Mitya began, but suddenly, as though beside himself, not knowing what he was doing, he cried out at the top of his voice:
“I un—der—stand!”
The young man in spectacles moved forward suddenly, and stepping up to Mitya, began with dignity, though hurriedly:
“We have to—in brief, I beg you to come this way, this way to the sofa. It's absolutely imperative that you give an explanation.”
“The old man!” cried Mitya frantically. “The old man and his blood! I understand.”
And he sank, almost fell, onto a chair close by, as though he had been mown down by a scythe.
“You understand? He understands it! Monster and parricide! Your father's blood cries out against you!” the old police captain suddenly roared, stepping up to Mitya.
He was beside himself, crimson in the face and trembling all over.
“This is impossible!” cried the small young man. “Mihail Makarovitch, Mihail Makarovitch, this won't do! Please allow me to speak. I would never have expected such behavior from you—”

“This is delirium, gentlemen, raving delirium,” cried the police captain. “Look at him: drunk, at this time of night, in the company of a disreputable woman, with the blood of his father on his hands. It's delirium!”
“I beg you most earnestly, dear Mihail Makarovitch, to restrain your feelings,” the prosecutor said in a rapid whisper to the old police captain, “or I shall be forced to resort to—”
But the little lawyer wouldn't let him finish. He turned to Mitya and delivered himself in a loud, firm, dignified voice:
“Ex-Lieutenant Karamazov, it is my duty to inform you that you are charged with the murder of your father, Fyodor Pavlovitch Karamazov, committed this night—”
He said something more, and the prosecutor put in something too, but though Mitya heard them, he didn't understand them. He stared at them all with wild eyes.
